readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Map paragraph jobs
readingWorkedEvidence.passage:
The instrument maker placed a row of finished flutes in her window. Passersby saw smooth tubes; the apprentice saw the shavings swept away before opening.

He proposed displaying the shavings too. The maker asked what a heap would explain. He sorted pieces by the operations that had produced them and laid an unfinished flute beside the rows.

A visitor followed the sequence with one finger. The apprentice moved his name card away from the center so it would not interrupt the path.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which paragraph map best captures the movement?
A. A finished product → an apprentice’s attempt to make it more decorative → a change in the shop’s prices
B. Different views of a product → a display that reveals the process → attention redirected toward that process
C. A maker’s objection → removal of the apprentice’s display → a visitor’s misunderstanding
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: Different views of a product → a display that reveals the process → attention redirected toward that process

Reason: The opening contrasts a finished object with its making; the middle organizes scraps into an explanation; the ending lets the visitor follow that sequence. The display does not change prices or disappear. Map the change in each paragraph’s role rather than treating an objection as the final outcome.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Separate topic from controlling claim
readingWorkedEvidence.passage:
Dark-colored roofs absorb much of the sunlight that strikes them. A reflective coating can reduce that absorbed energy, but its performance depends partly on what remains on the surface. Dust can cover the coating and alter its reflectance.

An engineer therefore compares both freshly coated and weathered panels. Her report treats reflectance as a property to maintain, not simply a number printed on a new product’s package.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which statement gives the controlling idea rather than only the subject?
A. The passage discusses reflective roof coatings.
B. Roof coatings should be selected entirely by the amount of dust nearby.
C. A coating’s cooling value depends on its continuing surface condition as well as its initial reflectance.
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: A coating’s cooling value depends on its continuing surface condition as well as its initial reflectance.

Reason: “Reflective roof coatings” names the subject but omits the development. The contrast between fresh and weathered panels supports a claim about maintained performance. Dust matters, but “entirely” discards the initial reflectance the passage also discusses. Build subject + what the writer establishes about it.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Keep the argumentative turn
readingWorkedEvidence.passage:
A school orchestra planned to perform an unfamiliar piece without an introduction, hoping listeners would encounter it without instructions about what to hear. During rehearsal, players disagreed about whether an abrupt silence was a joke or an interruption.

They recorded both versions and listened without the score. Neither sounded accidental. The conductor kept the silence but added a short spoken invitation to notice how the same pause might feel different on its return.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which summary keeps the full movement?
A. The orchestra moves from avoiding an introduction to briefly inviting listeners to notice the pause’s possible meanings.
B. The orchestra resolves the disagreement by removing the ambiguous pause from the piece.
C. A conductor replaces the players’ experiment with a detailed explanation of the correct interpretation.
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: The orchestra moves from avoiding an introduction to briefly inviting listeners to notice the pause’s possible meanings.

Reason: The passage moves from no introduction through two workable readings to a selective prompt. The pause remains and no single correct reading is imposed. A summary should carry the starting position, the complication, and the limited revision rather than invent resolution by removal or instruction.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Distinguish a true detail from the main idea
readingWorkedEvidence.passage:
A city greenhouse opened early on two weekdays so gardeners could collect seedlings before work. The early visitors came in small numbers, but many said they could not attend the usual afternoon hours. Some used the service repeatedly.

The manager recommended keeping one early morning rather than two. That schedule preserved an option for the gardeners while concentrating the limited staff time.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which accurate-sounding summary is too narrow?
A. The manager adjusts an access service to balance a particular need with limited staffing.
B. Some gardeners collected seedlings before work.
C. A small early-morning program is retained in a form that requires less staff time.
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: Some gardeners collected seedlings before work.

Reason: The middle statement is a true event, but it omits both the access problem and the scheduling decision. The other summaries account for the need and the adjustment. A detail does not become the main idea merely because it is stated explicitly. Ask what important part of the passage would remain unexplained if your choice were the title.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Infer narrative movement without inventing a moral
readingWorkedEvidence.passage:
Tess always took the highest path above the beach. From there she could reach home without sand in her shoes. When her younger cousin visited, she agreed to walk beside the pools and carried his shoes along with her own.

He stopped at each patch of water. Tess first watched the time, then crouched to see what held him. At the steps home she brushed both pairs of feet clean. The next morning she asked him whether the pools would still be full after breakfast.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
What change does the ending support?
A. Tess discovers that her cousin’s route is more efficient for reaching home.
B. Tess continues using the pools mainly to avoid disappointing her cousin.
C. Tess has developed an interest in a route she had previously avoided.
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: Tess has developed an interest in a route she had previously avoided.

Reason: The opening values the high path for avoiding sand. Crouching and asking about the next morning support a new interest, while cleaning feet preserves the inconvenience. The lower route is not established as more efficient, and the final invitation goes beyond merely accommodating a visitor.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Settle two close summaries with a pivot
readingWorkedEvidence.passage:
The curator’s draft called the restored dial “as its first owner saw it.” The conservator crossed out that phrase. The metal was original, but the hands had been replaced, and the lost glass was represented by a clear modern cover.

They kept the dial on display. The new caption named the surviving parts and distinguished them from the additions that made the object readable.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which detail separates “the restoration is rejected as inauthentic” from “the restoration is presented with its interventions made clear”?
A. The dial remains on display with additions identified.
B. The curator writes a first draft.
C. The dial once had an owner.
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: The dial remains on display with additions identified.

Reason: The two choices disagree about rejection versus qualified presentation. Keeping the object and identifying additions directly resolves that difference. Drafting and former ownership occur under either interpretation. When two summaries remain, locate the sentence on which their claims diverge instead of rereading every sentence equally.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Repair an overextended summary
readingWorkedEvidence.passage:
A botanist’s notebook described a hillside in spring. Her later essay used those notes to explain how she learned the names of flowers along one route. She wrote that naming made some differences easier to notice, though she continued to encounter forms she could not identify.

A student summarized the essay as proof that learning names gives a complete understanding of nature.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which repair matches the stated experience?
A. Naming replaces the need to keep observing the hillside.
B. Learning names changes the botanist’s attention without ending what she has yet to learn.
C. The essay shows that unidentified flowers are less important than named ones.
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: Learning names changes the botanist’s attention without ending what she has yet to learn.

Reason: “Complete understanding” conflicts with the continuing unidentified forms. A repaired summary retains the positive change—easier noticing—while removing the unsupported completion claim. Neither replacing observation nor ranking flowers is supported. The useful repair names the exact overreach and keeps the evidence the mistaken answer began with.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Map where a requested fact lives
readingWorkedEvidence.passage:
The island clinic sends supply orders on Mondays. A coastal office checks the orders on Tuesdays and combines them into one shipment. The ferry carries the boxes on Thursday unless weather closes the harbor.

Urgent medicine travels by a different arrangement; it does not wait for the weekly supply shipment.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
To find when routine supplies are physically transported, which part should you use?
A. The sentence about Monday orders
B. The exception for urgent medicine
C. The Thursday ferry sentence and its weather condition
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: The Thursday ferry sentence and its weather condition

Reason: The requested action is transport, not ordering or checking. Thursday supplies the time and the harbor exception qualifies it. Monday belongs to a different action, and urgent medicine is outside “routine supplies.” A location map connects each date to its own event before matching an answer.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Locate actor, action, and condition
readingWorkedEvidence.passage: Before opening the workshop, Ada tested the repaired lamp using a new bulb. The bulb lit, but the switch jammed on its second use. She set the lamp on a marked shelf and recorded the fault. Only after replacing the switch did she call its owner.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
When did Ada contact the owner?
A. After replacing the faulty switch
B. Immediately after the new bulb lit
C. When she first placed the lamp on the marked shelf
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: After replacing the faulty switch

Reason: The phrase “Only after replacing the switch” attaches directly to calling the owner. The bulb test and marked shelf are earlier real events, which makes them tempting. Match the question’s action—contacting—not simply the first successful test.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Read a stated cause without promoting sequence
readingWorkedEvidence.passage: A hall’s new entrance opened in September. Concert attendance rose in October, when the orchestra also began offering cheaper afternoon tickets. The hall manager attributed the rise to the ticket offer, based on answers collected from returning patrons. She said the entrance had made arrivals smoother but had not been the reason those patrons booked.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which explanation does the passage attribute to the manager?
A. The entrance caused the rise because it opened first.
B. The ticket offer prompted the reported patrons to book.
C. The entrance and tickets had equal effects on booking.
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: The ticket offer prompted the reported patrons to book.

Reason: The manager’s stated explanation concerns the ticket offer and the surveyed patrons. The entrance opening is earlier, but sequence alone does not make it her asserted cause. No equal division of effects is reported. A detail question can ask what a speaker says even when the passage is not proving that speaker’s account universally.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Keep a number attached to its denominator
readingWorkedEvidence.passage: The repair desk logged 36 visits involving 24 customers in one week. Nine visits were follow-ups on earlier work. The coordinator reported visits and customers in separate columns because one customer could return more than once.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which statement preserves the recorded quantity?
A. Thirty-six customers had items repaired.
B. Nine of the customers visited only for follow-up work.
C. The desk recorded thirty-six visits, some made by returning customers.
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: The desk recorded thirty-six visits, some made by returning customers.

Reason: Thirty-six counts visits, not unique customers. Nine also counts visits; it does not identify nine distinct people or establish their only reason for attending. The separate customer count is 24. Keep each value paired with its unit before paraphrasing it.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Preserve the strength of a paraphrase
readingWorkedEvidence.passage: The astronomer called the dimming pattern “compatible with a passing object” but noted that a change in the star itself had not been excluded. The report recommended observing another event before favoring either explanation.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which paraphrase is faithful?
A. A passing object remains a possible explanation, while an alternative still needs testing.
B. The pattern establishes that a passing object caused the dimming.
C. The report favors a change in the star over a passing object.
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: A passing object remains a possible explanation, while an alternative still needs testing.

Reason: “Compatible with” allows a passing object without selecting it as the cause. “Had not been excluded” preserves a stellar alternative, and the next observation is meant to help decide. Establishing one cause or favoring the other changes the report’s stated certainty.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Discriminate between adjacent dates
readingWorkedEvidence.passage: The committee approved the design in March and sent it for a safety review. Inspectors returned comments in April. The builder revised the railing in May, and the committee approved that revision in June. Work on the site began in July.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which date answers when the revised railing received approval?
A. May
B. June
C. July
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: June

Reason: May is when the builder changed the railing; June is when the committee approved that change; July is the start of construction. All are relevant to the project, but only June matches both “revised railing” and “approval.” Checking those two features is faster and safer than choosing the nearest remembered date.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Repair a speaker-and-scope error
readingWorkedEvidence.passage: The organizer predicted that the evening session would help all participants. After the first session, three attendees said its timing suited them; two other attendees did not submit comments. The report quoted the favorable comments but made no statement about the two who had not responded.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
How should “the report confirms that everyone preferred the evening” be corrected?
A. The organizer’s prediction is proved because favorable comments were received.
B. The two silent attendees opposed the timing.
C. Three attendees reported favorable timing; the other attendees’ views were not recorded.
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: Three attendees reported favorable timing; the other attendees’ views were not recorded.

Reason: The original prediction belongs to the organizer, while the report contains three comments and two unknown responses. Neither support nor opposition can be assigned to silent attendees. Repairing the error requires keeping speaker and sample scope separate, not merely weakening “everyone” to an equally invented count.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Separate observation from conclusion
readingWorkedEvidence.passage:
When the audience began clapping, Noor remained beside the wings with her program folded in her hand. A loose page lay beneath the last violinist’s chair. While other visitors moved toward the exit, she kept looking at the page.

After the players had left, she crossed the stage and picked it up. Outside, she caught up with the violinist and handed it over without introducing herself or mentioning the applause.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which inference about Noor’s reason for remaining has the clearest evidentiary link?
A. She wants the audience to recognize her role in the performance.
B. She remains at least partly so she can return the fallen page.
C. She and the violinist had arranged beforehand for her to collect the page.
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: She remains at least partly so she can return the fallen page.

Reason: Watching the page while others leave, then retrieving and returning it, supports a practical purpose for staying. The purpose is inferred from linked actions rather than stated directly. Public recognition and a prior arrangement add motives or events without a corresponding clue; at least partly avoids claiming this was her only reason.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Build a minimal motive from action
readingWorkedEvidence.passage: The potter packed the cracked trial pieces beside the finished bowls. When her student asked why, she placed the pieces in the order they had come from the kiln and pointed out where each firing had changed. She kept the finished bowls on the other side of the table.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Her arrangement most reasonably suggests that she wants the student to:
A. follow how the process was adjusted across attempts
B. identify the finished bowl most likely to reproduce an early firing defect
C. decide that the final bowls should be displayed without the discarded trials
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: follow how the process was adjusted across attempts

Reason: Ordering trials and pointing to changes supports following the process across attempts. Predicting a future defect or separating finished work from its developmental record would require another purpose that is not stated. The inference rests on the organized sequence the potter makes visible.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Distinguish a supported possibility from an invented one
readingWorkedEvidence.passage: The archivist requested photographs of the bindings before asking to borrow the books. A note on the loan form said that volumes with loose sewing would need supports during transport.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which inference needs the least extra information?
A. The archivist already knew every book had loose sewing.
B. The owners had refused an earlier loan request.
C. The archivist was checking what protection the books might need in transit.
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: The archivist was checking what protection the books might need in transit.

Reason: The request for binding photographs is linked to the stated transport condition. It supports checking possible protection needs, not certainty that every binding is loose. A prior refusal is possible but has no clue here. A good inference has a passage-specific reason, not merely a story that could explain the action.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Keep both halves of a mixed response
readingWorkedEvidence.passage: “That route would get us there before sunset,” Amari said. She drew her finger along the thin dotted path, then asked whether the footbridge had reopened after the storm. She put the map back on the table instead of folding it into her bag.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which attitude is best supported?
A. Determination to reject the route
B. Unreserved confidence that the route is ready
C. Interest in its advantage combined with concern about whether it is usable
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: Interest in its advantage combined with concern about whether it is usable

Reason: Arriving before sunset is a recognized advantage. Asking about the bridge and leaving the map open show an unresolved condition. Total rejection loses the benefit; unreserved confidence loses the practical concern. An attitude answer must explain the action as well as the positive or negative remark.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Use an explicit counterexample
readingWorkedEvidence.passage: A critic wrote that Ren’s new exhibition abandoned drawing for sculpture. The catalog listed four sculptures and twelve ink drawings. In an interview Ren said the sculptures began as a way to investigate spaces she had left blank on paper.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which claim is contradicted?
A. Ren has stopped exhibiting drawings.
B. Ren sees a connection between the two media.
C. The exhibition includes fewer sculptures than drawings.
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: Ren has stopped exhibiting drawings.

Reason: The twelve cataloged ink drawings directly contradict abandonment of exhibited drawing. The interview supports a connection between media, and four is fewer than twelve. A counterexample defeats a universal or exclusive claim without requiring you to settle every aspect of the artist’s intention.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Choose the clue that separates rival motives
readingWorkedEvidence.passage: Before releasing the family recording, Inez sent a copy to her cousin and asked him to mark any passage he did not want shared. She did not ask him to correct dates or identify voices.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which clue favors concern about consent over concern about factual accuracy?
A. She makes a copy of the recording.
B. She asks which passages he does not want shared.
C. The recording contains more than one voice.
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: She asks which passages he does not want shared.

Reason: Marking what may be shared is an action directed at permission. Copying and multiple voices could occur in either a consent check or an accuracy check. The explicit absence of date and identity questions reinforces the distinction. For two plausible motives, choose the clue that predicts one more specifically.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Repair the unsupported leap
readingWorkedEvidence.passage: After the demonstration, Eli asked to try the loom with a slower shuttle. The instructor brought one out, and Eli stayed after the scheduled finish to make another strip. A classmate concluded that he had decided to become a professional weaver.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which smaller conclusion is supported?
A. Eli has concluded that the demonstration method was ineffective.
B. Eli now intends to replace the instructor’s tools with his own.
C. Eli wanted another opportunity to work with an adjusted tool.
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: Eli wanted another opportunity to work with an adjusted tool.

Reason: Requesting a slower shuttle and continuing supports another attempt under adjusted conditions. It does not establish that the demonstrated method failed or a plan to replace the tools. The career claim in the prompt adds a future commitment beyond those observed actions.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Find the local object of the word
readingWorkedEvidence.passage: The geographer described the boundary as “porous.” Workers crossed it daily, families maintained homes on both sides, and merchants followed older routes that did not stop at the official markers. The line remained on the map.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
What does “porous” mean here?
A. Drawn with gaps in the printed ink
B. Able to admit movement across it
C. Made of material containing small physical holes
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: Able to admit movement across it

Reason: The following examples concern people and trade crossing a political line, while the mapped line remains. They support permeability to movement, not damaged printing or physical material. Locate what the adjective describes and use the nearby actions to choose its local sense.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Substitute before accepting a familiar sense
readingWorkedEvidence.passage: “The evidence will bear that interpretation,” the editor wrote, “but not the stronger claim that the author intended the ending to be comic.” She kept the interpretation and removed the claim about intention.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which substitute for “bear” preserves the sentence?
A. Support
B. Endure with discomfort
C. Produce as offspring
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: Support

Reason: The editor permits one interpretation because the evidence can support it, then rejects a stronger inference. “Endure” and “produce” are real senses of bear but do not connect evidence to a justified interpretation. Test the candidate in the actual sentence, including its contrast.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Let the contrast define the word
readingWorkedEvidence.passage: The first sketch spread ornament over every available edge. In the second, the border was “austere”: one dark line surrounded a wide blank margin. The artist had removed detail without changing the central scene.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which meaning does the contrast establish?
A. Carelessly unfinished
B. Severely simple
C. Old-fashioned in subject matter
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: Severely simple

Reason: The change from ornamented edges to a single line and blank margin defines a severe simplicity. The second sketch is deliberate, so unfinished carelessness is unsupported. The central scene does not change, so subject matter does not explain the adjective.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Read figurative action through its target
readingWorkedEvidence.passage: The old disagreement “shadowed” the committee’s later meetings. Even when a new proposal concerned another building, members returned to who had been trusted with the earlier plans. The room itself was brighter after renovation.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which meaning of “shadowed” fits?
A. Blocked light from reaching
B. Followed quietly without being noticed
C. Continued to influence in an unsettling way
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: Continued to influence in an unsettling way

Reason: The subject is an old disagreement and the result is repeated distrust, so the action is figurative influence. The brightened room explicitly makes literal light a poor fit; open returns to the dispute also exclude unnoticed following. Keep the emotional effect as well as the basic sense of continuing presence.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Check a meaning against the paragraph
readingWorkedEvidence.passage: The report called the bridge “sound.” It then described bolts that held their load, joints without visible movement, and a surface needing only a new finish. The engineers recommended painting rather than structural replacement.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which substitute fits the whole paragraph?
A. Structurally reliable
B. Producing a clear noise
C. Based on a persuasive argument
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: Structurally reliable

Reason: Bolts, joints, and the painting recommendation all concern physical condition. Structurally reliable fits every part. A noise or an argument can also be sound in another sense, but neither explains why replacement is unnecessary here. A local substitute must survive the paragraph, not just the word in isolation.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Settle two plausible neighboring senses
readingWorkedEvidence.passage: The critic called the new ending “restrained.” The central argument remained sharp, but the actor lowered her voice and let the final gesture finish without a speech. The critic praised the force of what was left unsaid.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which nearby evidence favors “controlled in expression” over “prevented from acting”?
A. The argument remains central.
B. The actor chooses a quieter delivery and ends without an added speech.
C. The review is published after the performance.
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: The actor chooses a quieter delivery and ends without an added speech.

Reason: The described delivery is a deliberate limit on expression that the critic praises, not an inability to act. A central argument could occur in either kind of performance, and publication timing does not define the word. Identify the feature on which the two possible senses differ.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Repair a subject-based dictionary guess
readingWorkedEvidence.passage: A student reading about a river chose “deposit of money” for “bank.” The sentence read: “The surveyors followed the bank until the reeds hid the water, then returned along a higher ridge.”
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which repair uses the contextual clue?
A. The river must run beside a financial business.
B. Bank means the bordering land, as shown by the route beside reeds and water.
C. Bank means a stored supply of reeds.
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: Bank means the bordering land, as shown by the route beside reeds and water.

Reason: The route runs beside water and is contrasted with a higher ridge, so the word names bordering land. Financial deposit is familiar but unsupported; a stored supply does not fit a route to follow. Repair the guess by naming the clue that rules in the local meaning rather than memorizing another isolated definition.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Map structure before naming a function
readingWorkedEvidence.passage:
The new mountain road appears as one continuous line joining the coastal town to the villages above it. At the opening, a council speaker called that line a connection for every home.

Rafi could drive his empty cart along the road, but with a full load of grain he stopped at its steepest turn. He carried several sacks around the bend before bringing the cart through.

A map can record a connection without showing the effort it demands from particular users. For Rafi, the road’s usefulness still depends on the cart’s load and the slope beneath its wheels.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which structural map fits?
A. Claim about connection → concrete difficulty → qualification of what connection means
B. General claim about travel → proof that the road has no useful purpose → a replacement route
C. A farmer’s difficulty → an account of why he caused it → confirmation of the opening claim
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: Claim about connection → concrete difficulty → qualification of what connection means

Reason: The farmer’s difficulty links a broad connection claim to the final qualification about usable access. The passage does not reject all usefulness or blame the farmer. Name how the middle changes the opening rather than restating its topic.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Explain why this detail is here
readingWorkedEvidence.passage: The miniature ship rewards a close look. Its maker carved not only the railings and rigging but also a latch inside a cupboard that visitors cannot open. That hidden fitting extends the precision of the model beyond anything the display ordinarily allows its audience to see.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
What is the latch detail’s main function?
A. To show why the cupboard should be opened for visitors
B. To give a concrete instance of workmanship extending beyond visible display
C. To identify a defect that weakens the claim of precision
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: To give a concrete instance of workmanship extending beyond visible display

Reason: The surrounding claim concerns precision beyond public sight, and the hidden latch exemplifies it. The essay neither requests access nor identifies a defect. Function connects a detail to the argument it supports; it is different from describing the object the detail mentions.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Match tone by direction and intensity
readingWorkedEvidence.passage:
This translation is an inviting beginning. Its clear opening gives a new reader room to follow the speaker without losing the abruptness of her questions.

Some later images, however, have become flatter. The small, sharp thing in the original sometimes becomes a broad word for brightness or movement. Those choices smooth the voice where its particularity matters.

I hope a later edition returns to these images. Because this edition makes the poem so approachable, I would welcome a revision that restores the sharper images.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which tone fits the treatment as a whole?
A. Dismissive of the translation’s usefulness
B. Confident that no revision is needed
C. Appreciative but constructively dissatisfied with some choices
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: Appreciative but constructively dissatisfied with some choices

Reason: “Inviting” and praise establish appreciation; the criticism and requested return establish dissatisfaction with specific choices. Dismissal ignores the praise, while complete satisfaction ignores a full paragraph and the closing wish. Tone must match both the evaluation’s direction and its measured intensity.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Separate the quoted claim from the author’s response
readingWorkedEvidence.passage:
“Machines have made the hand unnecessary,” a manufacturer announced at the fair. His advertisement showed the finished product sliding from a bright metal opening.

Behind the display, a worker paused the machine when its printed guide failed. She adjusted the feed wheel by touch, ran a test, and adjusted it again before allowing the product to continue.

The hand had not disappeared from this process. Which kinds of handwork, then, had the advertisement taught its visitors not to notice?
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Why does the essay include the manufacturer’s claim?
A. To introduce a position that the following observations complicate
B. To certify the claim as the essay’s own conclusion
C. To establish that the workers refused to use the machine
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: To introduce a position that the following observations complicate

Reason: The quoted assertion is followed by counterevidence: workers still use touch. The final question directly examines the advertisement’s framing. Quotation does not equal endorsement, and adjustment is not refusal to use the machine. Follow what the author does after another speaker’s words.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Explain an image’s selected relationship
readingWorkedEvidence.passage: At dusk the greenhouse panes became “a row of small moons” above the dark garden. Inside, workers moved seedlings from tray to tray; outside, the path had disappeared into shadow.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
What does the image chiefly emphasize?
A. The reflection of actual moonlight onto the workers
B. A separated line of pale light against surrounding darkness
C. A match between the workers’ movements and the regular spacing of the panes
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: A separated line of pale light against surrounding darkness

Reason: The shared feature is a row of pale lights against darkness, reinforced by the shadowed path. The image does not identify the physical source as moonlight or align the workers’ movements with the panes. Explain the selected visual relationship rather than adding another part of the scene.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Distinguish example, concession, and reversal
readingWorkedEvidence.passage: I want the old stairway to remain available. It is narrow, and carrying boxes up it is awkward. But the new side entrance can handle deliveries while the stair stays open for ordinary use. Preserving it need not require pretending that every task belongs on it.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
What does the admission do?
A. It withdraws the argument for keeping the stairs.
B. It supplies the main benefit of the old design.
C. It acknowledges a practical objection that the proposed arrangement addresses.
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: It acknowledges a practical objection that the proposed arrangement addresses.

Reason: The inconvenience is a concession, not the author’s reason for preservation. The next sentence offers an answer without reversing the position. Use the neighboring sentences to distinguish an acknowledged problem from abandonment of the claim.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Repair a purpose answer that only retells
readingWorkedEvidence.passage:
Before leaving, I checked the forecast three times. The same chance of showers remained on the screen; I wanted a more cooperative answer. I finally put the phone away and hurried toward the club.

When rain began, I kept going. By the time I arrived, my sleeves were wet, my shoes made a noise on the floor, and I was laughing.

A student labels the first paragraph’s purpose “to tell us that the narrator checks the weather.”
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which revision explains its role rather than repeating its content?
A. It contrasts the narrator’s early wish to avoid rain with the later laughter despite getting wet.
B. It establishes the checks as evidence that the later rain was forecast accurately.
C. It shows why reaching the club depends on obtaining a different forecast.
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: It contrasts the narrator’s early wish to avoid rain with the later laughter despite getting wet.

Reason: Wanting a more cooperative forecast supplies evidence of a wish for a manageable outcome; later laughter in the rain changes that response. The task is not to establish forecast accuracy or a condition for reaching the club. Connecting the first paragraph to the later response explains its role rather than merely repeating the weather-checking action.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Map each claim before finding overlap
readingWorkedEvidence.passage:
Source A: The new route shortens the walk from the station to the clinic. Its value is the direct connection it creates.

Source B: A shorter walk helps only if people can use the surface throughout the year. I support the route, but its drainage must be funded as part of construction.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which two-column map is faithful?
A. A: a direct route matters; B: drainage must be funded as part of building it
B. A: a direct route matters only after drainage is funded; B: a shorter walk is sufficient by itself
C. A: the clinic’s distance is irrelevant; B: the drainage question should be postponed until after construction
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: A: a direct route matters; B: drainage must be funded as part of building it

Reason: A emphasizes a shorter connection. B accepts its benefit but requires drainage to be part of the construction plan. The wrong maps transfer a condition to the wrong writer, reverse its force, or remove the benefit A actually stresses.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Retain the precise difference between supporters
readingWorkedEvidence.passage: Writer A supports publishing the letters so readers can encounter the correspondence directly. Writer B also supports publication, provided the edition identifies missing pages and distinguishes uncertain dates from confirmed ones. Neither argues for rewriting the letters.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Where do the positions differ?
A. Whether publishing the letters is useful without any new research about their authors
B. Whether a complete-looking edition is preferable to one that marks its gaps
C. B explicitly requires documentation of gaps and uncertain dates.
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: B explicitly requires documentation of gaps and uncertain dates.

Reason: Both support publication. B explicitly adds documentation of missing pages and uncertain dates; the text does not establish an opposing preference by A for concealment. The distinction is a stated condition, not an invented disagreement inferred from A’s silence.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Combine compatible claims without inventing a verdict
readingWorkedEvidence.passage: A landscape study reports that the planted strip reduced wind speed at the field edge. A second report finds that the strip occupies land previously used for crops, but does not calculate the value of either the lost crop area or the wind protection.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which joint conclusion follows?
A. The protection is worth more than the lost crop area.
B. The strip provides measured wind protection while the overall economic tradeoff remains uncalculated.
C. The loss of crop area cancels the measured wind reduction.
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: The strip provides measured wind protection while the overall economic tradeoff remains uncalculated.

Reason: The sources establish a physical benefit and a cost in land use, not their relative economic values. They can both be true without canceling one another. A combined answer may retain an unresolved tradeoff; it must not create a cost-benefit verdict absent from either source.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Read the table’s unit before making the claim
readingWorkedEvidence.passage:
The gallery records each doorway entry, including a person returning after leaving.

Day — Doorway entries
Friday — 120
Saturday — 150

A companion note explains that workshop participants often left for lunch and returned through the same doors. The table therefore counts entry events rather than assigning a new identity to each event.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which claim uses both the table and definition correctly?
A. The gallery had thirty more distinct visitors on Saturday.
B. Twenty-five percent of Saturday visitors attended the workshop.
C. Saturday had thirty more entries, but the figures do not identify the change in distinct visitors.
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: Saturday had thirty more entries, but the figures do not identify the change in distinct visitors.

Reason: Subtract like units: 150 − 120 = 30 entries. Repeat entry means that difference is not automatically thirty new people. Workshop behavior explains a possible difference between measures but gives no percentage of visitors. Both the numeric operation and the unit definition must survive the combined claim.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Respect the intersection of study limits
readingWorkedEvidence.passage: Study A found improved recall for adults learning short lists aloud. Study B found improved recall for teenagers practicing pictures silently. Neither study compared the two methods in the same participants, and neither measured retention after a week.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which combined conclusion stays inside both studies?
A. A benefit occurred under each tested method and group, without establishing which method lasts longer.
B. Speaking is equally effective for adults and teenagers.
C. The two studies prove that both methods preserve learning for a week.
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: A benefit occurred under each tested method and group, without establishing which method lasts longer.

Reason: A and B each support a benefit in their own tested conditions. Different groups and materials prevent assigning their difference solely to method, and neither measures week-long retention. Combining positive results does not erase limits, create an age comparison, or supply an unmeasured time period.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Use the exact point of disagreement
readingWorkedEvidence.passage: Historian A treats a merchant’s list as a record of goods intended for shipment. Historian B agrees about that purpose but warns that the list alone does not establish which goods arrived; she asks to compare a receiving ledger.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which evidence would most directly address B’s additional question?
A. A second copy confirming which goods the merchant intended to send
B. A ledger identifying the goods received at the destination
C. A ledger showing what similar merchants sent to other destinations
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: A ledger identifying the goods received at the destination

Reason: B asks which goods arrived in this shipment. Another plan confirms intention, and other merchants’ records provide a comparison without documenting this delivery. The receiving ledger addresses the precise step B wants checked.

readingWorkedEvidence.title: Worked method: Repair a merged-speaker conclusion
readingWorkedEvidence.passage: A designer says the square should retain its old benches because people recognize them as meeting places. A wheelchair user supports retaining some, but asks for spaces beside them wide enough for different seating needs. A summary says both oppose changing the bench area.
readingWorkedEvidence.task:
Which repair preserves both positions?
A. Both think recognition is the only important consideration.
B. The wheelchair user rejects retaining any old benches.
C. Both allow old benches to remain, while the wheelchair user also calls for changes around them.
readingWorkedEvidence.solution:
Supported answer: Both allow old benches to remain, while the wheelchair user also calls for changes around them.

Reason: Retaining benches is the overlap; changing adjacent space is the added condition. The mistaken summary turns agreement about an object into agreement against every alteration. Repair by naming each speaker’s actual scope instead of treating all support for preservation as opposition to change.

skillCards.title: Find the controlling claim rather than only a subject
Preserve the passage’s argumentative movement
Match a summary to its scope and qualifications
Trace a specific narrative change without overgeneralizing
Locate the exact actor, action, and requested fact
Separate the stated sequence and explanation
Keep the speaker, unit, denominator, and condition
Preserve the meaning and strength of a paraphrase
Build the smallest conclusion from a specific clue
Separate a supported inference from a plausible added story
Infer an attitude while preserving mixed feelings
Test a claim with an explicit contradiction or alternative
Choose the word’s local sense and grammatical role
Use a neighboring contrast or example to define a word
Follow the target of a figurative action
Verify the substitute against the paragraph’s claim
Explain a detail’s job in its surrounding argument
Match the direction and intensity of the writer’s tone
Track speakers, concessions, and structural shifts
Explain an image’s effect without importing extra properties
Compare the writers’ shared aims and exact differences
Combine sources or distant details without inventing a verdict
Match a graphic’s values, units, and comparison base
Keep the combined conclusion within every source’s limits
Read the requested quantity, sample, and unit
body: Name the quantity requested, its unit, and the treatment or time. Match the table column or graph axis before comparing values. In a graph, use the legend to select the correct series.
A final amount, a change, and a rate answer different questions. Reading the largest number without its label can select the wrong quantity.

activity.prompt: A thermometer table lists elapsed time and temperature. Which column answers “how warm at 4 min”?
activity.explanation: The question asks for temperature at a specified time. Time selects the row; temperature is the requested output.
activity.evidenceText: Trial 1: at 4 min the sample is 32°C and has volume 50 mL.

skillCards.title: Subtract baselines and keep the fraction denominator
body: Change = final − initial. Amount removed = initial − final. Fraction removed divides the removed amount by the initial amount; fraction remaining divides the final amount by the initial amount.
Percentage-point change subtracts percentages. Relative percent change divides that difference by the original percentage. A rate additionally divides a change by elapsed time.

activity.prompt: A sample falls from 50 to 20 mg/L. What percentage of its initial concentration was removed?
activity.explanation: Removal is 50−20 = 30 mg/L. Divide by the initial 50, not the remaining 20: 30/50 = 60%.
activity.evidenceText: Concentration: initial 50 mg/L; final 20 mg/L; volume unchanged.

skillCards.title: Check every threshold, including equality
body: Turn every requirement into a separate test. “At least” includes equality; “greater than” does not. Eliminate a candidate as soon as it fails a required condition.
Write ratios in the requested direction. Output per area means output/area. Reversing numerator and denominator changes both the units and the ranking.

activity.prompt: Which water sample meets BOTH temperature below 25°C and oxygen at least 6 mg/L?
activity.explanation: M has 24°C and 6 mg/L and passes both. N fails the strict temperature limit; O fails the oxygen minimum.

skillCards.title: Normalize counts, areas, and volumes before ranking
body: Counts measure totals; densities measure counts per area or volume. Divide before ranking samples of unequal sizes. If every sample has the same size, counts and densities rank them alike.
A percentage needs its own denominator. Percent germinated uses all starting seeds; mean root length might include only seedlings that sprouted. Read the study definition.

activity.prompt: Which pool has the greater insect density?
activity.explanation: U has 24/3 = 8 insects/L; V has 30/6 = 5 insects/L. Dividing by volume makes the samples comparable.
activity.evidenceText: U: 24 insects in 3 L. V: 30 insects in 6 L.

skillCards.title: Compare interval changes and distinguish period from duration
body: For a measured change, subtract the two outputs and divide by the elapsed interval if the question asks for a rate. Equal total changes over unequal intervals give different rates.

A repeating period is the interval between matching events, such as successive peaks; the duration of one isolated dip is not a repeat period. A record containing only one event cannot establish the time until its repetition.

activity.prompt: A population rises from 120 at hour 2 to 180 at hour 5. What is its average increase per hour?
activity.explanation: Use change divided by elapsed time: (180−120)/(5−2) = 60/3 = 20 organisms/h.
activity.evidenceText: Population: hour 2 = 120; hour 5 = 180.

skillCards.title: Calculate a supplied model before comparing outputs
body: Write the supplied rule with the column names beside its inputs. Calculate the requested output for every candidate, keeping its units, before ranking results. The largest single input need not give the largest product or ratio.
If the question changes an input, recompute from the rule while keeping the stated constants fixed. A temperature change, final temperature, and energy amount are different outputs.

activity.prompt: For the supplied output P = VI, which device has greater power?
activity.explanation: D gives 4×9 = 36 mW; E gives 6×5 = 30 mW. Compare products rather than voltage alone.
activity.evidenceText: D: 4 V, 9 mA. E: 6 V, 5 mA. Voltage × current in these units gives mW.

skillCards.title: Combine flows and use weighted concentration
body: Compute the quantity requested before ranking samples. A supplied equation may require multiplying two columns, subtracting a baseline, or dividing by another quantity. Keep units through the calculation; the largest individual input need not give the largest output.

When streams mix, add pollutant mass flows and divide by total water flow. Weight concentration by flow rather than averaging concentrations equally. Match sample, time, and units when combining presentations.

activity.prompt: A supplies 12 L/s at 2 mg/L and B supplies 4 L/s at 10 mg/L. What concentration follows complete mixing?
activity.explanation: Mass flow is 12×2+4×10 = 64 mg/s. Water flow is 16 L/s. The flow-weighted concentration is 64/16 = 4 mg/L.
activity.evidenceText: The solute is conserved and both streams are completely mixed.

skillCards.title: Chain calibration, dilution, and a changed flow
body: Follow the whole measurement chain: signal → calibrated concentration in the measured liquid → original concentration after undoing dilution → mass carried per time. Keep the sample identity and units at every step.
A flow change affects mass per time even if concentration stays fixed. Compare the requested final quantities only after each sample’s own corrections are complete.

activity.prompt: After its flow is halved, how much pollutant does Stream A carry each second?
activity.explanation: Signal 2 gives C = 3×2 = 6 mg/L in the diluted liquid; threefold dilution means original C = 18 mg/L. New flow is 1 L/s, so mass flow is 18 mg/s.
activity.evidenceText: Calibration C = 3S mg/L. A has S = 2 after threefold dilution and original flow 2 L/s; no solute is lost. Only flow is halved.

skillCards.title: Interpolate between the nearest bounding measurements
body: Interpolation estimates an output between measured inputs. For a straight segment, find the fraction of the horizontal gap traveled and apply that fraction to the vertical change.
Use the nearest bounding points rather than averaging every measurement. If the question supplies a different model, follow that model instead.

activity.prompt: Using straight-line interpolation, estimate the temperature at 7 min.
activity.explanation: Seven minutes is halfway from 5 to 9 min, so use the midpoint of 46 and 34: (46+34)/2 = 40°C.
activity.evidenceText: A different sample is 46°C at 5 min and 34°C at 9 min.

skillCards.title: Compare changes using the actual interval lengths
body: For equal input intervals, compare successive output changes. For unequal intervals, divide each change by its interval length before comparing rates.
Direction and rate are separate. A temperature can keep falling while its cooling slows. Use the signed slope for direction and its magnitude for speed of change.

activity.prompt: Which interval has the greater average cooling rate in magnitude?
choices: Neither interval, because only instantaneous rates can be compared
activity.explanation: Compare temperature change divided by interval length: the first magnitude is 16/2 = 8°C/min and the second is 18/6 = 3°C/min. The second total drop is larger, but it takes three times as long. Falling in both intervals does not make the rates equal, and average rates can be compared without instantaneous measurements.
activity.evidenceText: At 0, 2, and 8 min, a sample is 70, 54, and 36°C.

skillCards.title: Limit maxima and predictions to the tested domain
body: A tested maximum is the largest measured result, not necessarily the exact optimum. Measurements on either side of a peak can narrow the search without locating every untested point.
Beyond the observed range, a prediction is extrapolation. A plateau does not prove a permanent limit, and an increasing segment does not justify “always increases.”

activity.prompt: A response is 4, 11, and 8 at doses 1, 3, and 5. Which claim is supported?
choices: Dose 3 has the largest measured response
The true maximum must occur exactly at dose 3
Response increases throughout the interval from dose 1 to dose 5
The response at dose 4 is known to be exactly 9.5
activity.explanation: Among the three measured outputs, 11 at dose 3 is largest. The fall to 8 at dose 5 contradicts a continuously increasing claim. No measurements locate an exact overall optimum or establish a straight-line value of 9.5 at dose 4; those add claims beyond the observations.
activity.evidenceText: All three doses are measured in the same units under the same conditions.

skillCards.title: Separate slope, intercept, ratios, and direct proportion
body: Slope is output change divided by input change. An intercept is the predicted output at input zero; a nonzero intercept prevents absolute outputs from being directly proportional to inputs.
When a question asks for an added amount, subtract the baseline before comparing ratios. An equation may describe a range rather than every possible condition.

activity.prompt: For T = 18−3d, what is the temperature change per meter?
activity.explanation: The coefficient of d is the slope: each additional meter lowers temperature by 3°C. The 18°C intercept is the value at zero depth.
activity.evidenceText: Temperature T is in °C and depth d is in meters.

skillCards.title: Use the stated nonlinear model and the requested output
body: A straight segment and a nonlinear equation are different assumptions. Substitute the requested input into the stated equation rather than silently replacing it with a line.
For a squared relationship, changing an input by a factor changes its square by that factor squared. Check whether the equation predicts distance, squared distance, or time.

activity.prompt: For x² = 9t, what distance is predicted at 16 min?
activity.explanation: Substitute t = 16: x² = 144. The nonnegative distance is √144 = 12 mm; 144 is squared distance.
activity.evidenceText: The supplied model uses x in mm and t in minutes.

skillCards.title: Distinguish turning points, plateaus, and later evidence
body: Compare successive changes to distinguish a plateau, a turning point, and a steady trend. A turning point reverses direction; a plateau has little further change.
Check whether an instrument saturates before explaining a flat signal as a biological limit. Different measured responses can have different peaks or directions.

activity.prompt: Which series has a turning point rather than only slowing growth?
activity.explanation: The selected series rises to 10 and then falls to 6, so its direction reverses. Smaller positive increases alone do not create a turning point.
activity.evidenceText: All series have equal input spacing.

skillCards.title: Identify a variable and its matched baseline control
body: The independent variable is deliberately changed; the dependent variable is measured. Controlled variables are held fixed. A control group supplies the comparison needed for the stated question.
A zero-dose group can still contain naturally occurring material. A vehicle-only group receives the inactive carrier so that its effect is separated from the active ingredient.

activity.prompt: To test the active drug dissolved in oil, what should the comparison group receive?
choices: The same oil without the drug
activity.explanation: An oil-only control holds the carrier constant. Comparing against no oil changes both drug presence and carrier presence.
activity.evidenceText: The outcome is measured after equal times, with otherwise matched groups.

skillCards.title: Remove the second factor that changes with treatment
body: A confound is another relevant factor that changes alongside the treatment. A result from two simultaneous changes cannot identify either change as the sole cause.
Split one source material among separate units, assign treatments randomly, and keep other relevant conditions comparable. More repeats alone do not repair a built-in confound.

activity.prompt: Heated pots receive more water than cool pots. Which change most directly isolates heating?
choices: Use the same water amount in both groups
Use a more precise thermometer in both groups
activity.explanation: Heating and water amount currently vary together. Giving both groups the same water isolates heating. More measurements, more heated pots, or a more precise thermometer can improve sampling or precision while leaving the water confound intact.
activity.evidenceText: All other conditions are already held constant.

skillCards.title: Choose the comparison that tests the stated factor
body: Translate the hypothesis into the one factor that must differ. Keep the response definition and endpoint matched. A no-treatment control tests adding a treatment; equal treatment amounts with different forms can isolate a property such as surface area.
A group mean describes the tested group, not every individual. Keep a conclusion within the tested population, time, and conditions; a well-controlled comparison does not establish all environments.

activity.prompt: To test whether stirring changes dissolving time, which pair is best?
choices: Stirred hot water versus unstirred cold water
Equal masses and water temperatures; stirred versus unstirred
Stirred water with twice the solid versus unstirred water with the original solid mass
Two stirred cups at different temperatures
activity.explanation: Compare stirred and unstirred cups at the same solid mass and water temperature. Equal water volumes and a shared endpoint complete the control. Changing temperature or mass with stirring mixes causes, while two stirred cups do not test stirring at all.
activity.evidenceText: All cups contain equal water volumes, and dissolving time uses the same endpoint in every cup.

skillCards.title: Count independently treated units and within-unit readings
body: The experimental unit is the object or group independently assigned a treatment. Multiple readings of the same object are repeated measurements, not extra independent treatment units.
Replication estimates consistency across units. Random assignment reduces systematic starting differences; neither automatically removes an uncontrolled treatment difference.

activity.prompt: Three independently treated trays each contain 12 seedlings. How many experimental units received treatment independently?
activity.explanation: Treatment was assigned to trays, so the independent units are the three trays. More seedlings improve sampling within a tray but do not create more treatment assignments.
activity.evidenceText: One treatment is applied to an entire tray; individual seedlings are not assigned separate treatments.

skillCards.title: Distinguish blinding, assignment, and exposure history
body: Random assignment addresses starting-group differences. Blinding hides labels from scorers to reduce expectation bias. Counterbalancing varies treatment order; fresh groups or adequate recovery address carryover. These are different design decisions.
Identify the suspected bias first, then choose the change that directly targets it. More observations in the same fixed order do not test whether order caused the difference.

activity.prompt: Which change most directly tests whether receiving A first affected the later B response?
choices: Score the same A→B videos without labels
Record A→B at twice the frame rate
activity.explanation: Reversing order creates the missing comparison. Blinding targets scoring expectations, and a faster recording leaves the same exposure order in place.
activity.evidenceText: All animals currently receive A before B. Treatment durations and scoring procedures are otherwise matched.

skillCards.title: Compare treatment effects across contexts
body: To estimate one factor’s effect, hold the other fixed. Compare those effects across the other factor’s levels to test context dependence. When groups start at different values, compare each group’s before-to-after change before comparing the groups.
A useful follow-up includes missing matched conditions. Changing duration, sample type, and treatment together creates a new confound instead of resolving the old one.

activity.prompt: Which condition has the larger treatment-minus-control effect?
activity.explanation: Low light gives 8−3 = 5; high light gives 11−9 = 2. A larger final treated value need not mean a larger treatment effect.
activity.evidenceText: Low light: control 3, treated 8. High light: control 9, treated 11. All values use the same response unit.

skillCards.title: Define the response and distinguish accuracy from resolution
body: An operational definition specifies exactly how a response is measured. Precision means repeated values cluster together; accuracy means they are near an accepted reference. A tightly clustered offset can be precise yet inaccurate.

Repetition can reduce random uncertainty in a mean, but it does not remove a systematic calibration error. Test an accepted standard, correct the offset, and use an instrument fine enough to resolve the proposed difference.

activity.prompt: A ruler marked only every 1 cm is used to compare lengths expected to differ by 0.2 cm. What is the most direct improvement?
choices: Read the same coarse mark more times
Use a ruler with finer graduations
Measure twice as many samples with the same coarse ruler
Use a calibrated ruler with the same 1 cm graduations
activity.explanation: Finer graduations directly improve resolution of the expected 0.2 cm difference. Repetition or more samples does not give an individual reading finer marks. Calibration addresses systematic accuracy, but a calibrated ruler with the same coarse graduations still has the stated resolution limit.
activity.evidenceText: The study otherwise uses independent replicates and consistent measurement endpoints.

skillCards.title: Keep conclusions within the measured groups and conditions
body: A controlled comparison supports a conclusion about its tested units, response, duration, and conditions. A mean is a group summary, not a claim that each unit changed by exactly that amount.
Separate observed differences from unmeasured mechanisms or future settings. Keeping conditions matched strengthens the test without making its result universal.

activity.prompt: Which conclusion stays within the study?
choices: Every treated seedling gained exactly 2 g
The treatment had the larger mean mass under the tested conditions
The treatment will have the same effect in every soil
activity.explanation: The means differ by 2 g in the stated experiment. Means do not give every individual result, and one soil/time combination does not establish every soil.
activity.evidenceText: One species in one soil for 10 days: control mean final mass 5 g, treated mean 7 g. Individual values were not identical.

skillCards.title: Translate each mechanism into its stated prediction
body: Name the phenomenon, then write cause → expected observation for each viewpoint. Keep reported facts separate from proposed mechanisms. A group’s most common response is its mode, not a claim that every individual responded identically. A mode can also be fewer than half the observations.
A shared prediction cannot distinguish explanations. Seek a condition where predicted outcomes differ rather than merely a fact mentioned by one author.

activity.prompt: F proposes trapped air; G proposes newly formed oxygen. Which observation alone is shared and therefore weak for separating them?
choices: Gas is mostly oxygen absent initially
Bubbling persists after dissolved air is removed
activity.explanation: Both mechanisms can produce visible bubbles. Their chemical source, not the presence of bubbles, is the disagreement.
activity.evidenceText: Both accounts explicitly predict visible bubbles, but propose different gas sources.

skillCards.title: Test a mechanism without changing the competing cause
body: A removal-and-restoration comparison is strongest when the manipulation leaves the competing cause unchanged. Otherwise the intervention may change both explanations at once.
A result can favor a causal contribution without proving every molecular detail or eliminating every alternative. State the supported link at the level actually tested.

activity.prompt: An inhibitor lowers light output, but also blocks oxygen supply. Why is a chemical-only conclusion uncertain?
choices: The chemical process must be the only cause because light output decreased
Oxygen supply changed along with the chemical process
The oxygen mechanism must be correct because oxygen delivery decreased
Repeating the same manipulation would separate the two mechanisms
activity.explanation: The manipulation changes both a chemical process and oxygen delivery, each relevant to a competing explanation. The fall in light output therefore cannot be assigned uniquely to either. Repeating that confounded manipulation does not separate them; a control preserving oxygen delivery while inhibiting the chemical would be more informative.
activity.evidenceText: One hypothesis requires the inhibited chemical; the competing hypothesis requires oxygen delivery.

skillCards.title: Distinguish feasible transport from the route that occurred
body: Showing that a process can occur establishes feasibility; it does not show that it caused one historical event. A necessary condition must be met, but meeting it is not sufficient proof.
Choose evidence that documents the disputed event or eliminates a required condition. Avoid converting “possible” into “definitely happened.”

activity.prompt: Rock fragments survive both river transport and glacier transport. What follows about a particular deposit?
activity.explanation: Survival demonstrates that either process could deliver fragments. Evidence about the particular deposit is still required to choose its actual history.
activity.evidenceText: No transport traces or historical observations are supplied.

skillCards.title: Compare viewpoints under one matched condition
body: Hold a competing factor fixed while testing the claimed factor. In a two-factor table, compare rows or columns differing in only the relevant condition. When comparing proportions, identify each sample denominator; a larger count need not mean a larger fraction.
A predicted relationship can match while its internal mechanism remains untested. Distinguish the response pattern from an explanation of how it occurs.

activity.prompt: To test a humidity-driven explanation against a light-driven one, which comparison isolates humidity?
activity.explanation: Hold light fixed and change humidity so that a response difference targets humidity. Changing both factors mixes the predictions.
activity.evidenceText: Other relevant conditions and measurement time remain constant.

skillCards.title: Choose evidence or cue settings that separate predictions
body: Two explanations may agree under ordinary conditions. Change one cue or input while keeping the alternative cue fixed to create different predicted outcomes.
For three viewpoints, compare the pair named in the question first. Evidence that rejects one explanation may remain consistent with two others.

activity.prompt: Both models predict 6 at setting A but predict 9 and 15 at B. Which setting is more informative?
choices: Neither, because a model must match every setting before it can be tested
activity.explanation: At B the models make different predictions, 9 and 15, so an adequate measurement can distinguish them. Both predict 6 at A; measuring that shared prediction more precisely does not separate them. A model need not first be shown correct at all settings before an informative test is possible.
activity.evidenceText: The two settings are equally measurable and within both models’ stated ranges.

skillCards.title: Check the separate components of a combined mechanism
body: Split a compound explanation into its requirements, match each to evidence, and look for a contradiction. Shared evidence, separating evidence, and unmeasured conditions serve different roles.
When new information changes a background condition, carry it into each model’s prediction. Support requires the complete claim to fit, not just one convenient observation.

activity.prompt: A model claims germination needs both dry soil and warmth. Germination occurs in warm wet soil. Which claim is contradicted by this observation?
choices: Warmth and dry soil together are sufficient
activity.explanation: Germination in wet soil is a counterexample to dry soil being necessary. Warmth is present, so its necessity is not contradicted. A result under a different set of conditions also does not disprove that dry soil alone, or warm dry soil, could be sufficient; necessity and sufficiency are distinct claims.
activity.evidenceText: The germination observation and soil moisture measurement are reliable.

skillCards.title: Compute the exact prediction and compare every row
body: A model is a specified rule, not merely a direction of change. Substitute the input and compare predicted with observed output under the same conditions and units.
One point where two models agree does not separate them. Use another input where their numerical predictions differ.

activity.prompt: Model R predicts y = 4x+2. What is its prediction at x = 3?
activity.explanation: Substitute into the complete expression: 4×3+2 = 14. Omitting the intercept gives 12, which is a different model.
activity.evidenceText: x and y are dimensionless measured quantities.

skillCards.title: Distinguish fixed additions from repeated factors
body: Linear change adds equal amounts over equal input steps. Exponential change multiplies by an equal factor; direct proportion also requires a constant output/input ratio and zero intercept.
Write intermediate steps to avoid counting growth intervals incorrectly. A constant percentage change need not give constant absolute differences.

activity.prompt: A substance retains one third each hour. Starting at 81 mg, how much remains after 3 h?
activity.explanation: Apply the factor three times: 81→27→9→3 mg. Subtracting 3 mg per hour would model a different process.
activity.evidenceText: The same one-hour retention factor applies in each interval.

skillCards.title: Challenge a model inside its stated conditions
body: Test a claim within its stated input range and relevant conditions. A mismatch there challenges the model; a result outside that domain may instead reveal that the model cannot be extended.
Matching measured data supports the rule under tested conditions. It does not prove every material, time period, or untested environment.

activity.prompt: A model applies at 10–30°C. Which observation tests its claim most directly?
choices: A result from a different material outside its scope
activity.explanation: Twenty-two degrees lies within the stated domain and holds the modeled material fixed. The other choices test an unsupported extension.
activity.evidenceText: All other model conditions are met for the 22°C trial.

skillCards.title: Apply exponents and reciprocal factor changes
body: Treat each changed factor separately, including exponents and denominator effects, then multiply the factors. Hold all unchanged quantities fixed.
Use units to identify the actual output. A reciprocal equation predicts the reciprocal first; a squared equation predicts a square before taking a root.

activity.prompt: For R = kL/A, length doubles and area quadruples. What happens to resistance R?
activity.explanation: The length change gives ×2 and the area change gives ÷4. Together, 2/4 = 1/2, with k held constant.
activity.evidenceText: The same material and temperature keep k constant.

skillCards.title: Choose inputs where the model predictions diverge
body: Calculate each model’s prediction at the same candidate input. A point of agreement cannot separate them even if it is measured very precisely. Choose a valid input where their predictions differ.
Keep the test inside the stated domains and its measurement resolution adequate for the difference. Repeating a shared prediction can check consistency without deciding which rule is right.

activity.prompt: Which input separates the predictions?
choices: Both give identical predictions at every x
activity.explanation: At x = 1 both give 5. At x = 2, A gives 7 and B gives 9, so that setting can separate them.
activity.evidenceText: Model A: y = 2x+3. Model B: y = 4x+1. Both apply at x = 1 and x = 2, and output can be resolved to 0.1 unit.

skillCards.title: Identify the limit of a saturating model
body: A saturating model approaches a limit while a proportional model grows without bound. Choose a valid input where their predictions differ enough to measure.

Account for rounding and measurement uncertainty when judging a mismatch. Do not invent statistical significance from means alone; a meaningful comparison needs appropriate information about variability.

activity.prompt: For q = 8C/(3+C), what value is approached as positive C becomes very large?
activity.explanation: Divide by C: q = 8/(3/C+1). The 3/C term approaches zero, so q approaches 8 from below.
activity.evidenceText: C is positive; the model is assumed applicable at large C for this question.

skillCards.title: Correct the baseline before computing a decay fraction
body: Identify raw totals versus the signal of interest. Subtract a background before comparing the corrected signal, and add it back if the question asks for a raw future reading.
Net biological change likewise combines gains and losses. A zero net change may hide equal nonzero production and consumption.

activity.prompt: Raw readings are 255 then 130 with constant background 5. What happens to the corrected signal?
activity.explanation: Subtract background from each reading: 255−5 = 250 and 130−5 = 125. The corrected signal halves. Halving the initial raw reading gives 127.5 rather than the observed corrected value; adding background gives 260 and 135; leaving both raw values unchanged omits the correction.
activity.evidenceText: The detector background remains 5 counts/min throughout.

skillCards.title: Use all experiments and choose a matched follow-up
body: A model must fit all relevant observations under matched conditions. A second table can change the interpretation of the first, such as revealing a shared offset or a nutrient-dependent effect.
Choose a follow-up that separates explanations while preserving controls. Merely repeating an agreement point improves measurement consistency but may not test the disputed mechanism.

activity.prompt: Model A fits Experiment 1 but contradicts reliable Experiment 2 under its own stated conditions. What is justified?
choices: Its first success is sufficient to retain the original claim unchanged
Its original stated claim remains valid if Experiment 2 is omitted from the fit
A model that fits Experiment 2 must automatically explain Experiment 1
The model needs revision despite its first success
activity.explanation: Both experiments are reliable and satisfy the stated conditions, so the second contradiction requires revision despite the first success. Omitting a contradictory in-scope test does not repair the claim. A competing model must also face both datasets; fitting one does not automatically establish a fit to the other.
activity.evidenceText: Both experiments satisfy the model’s stated conditions and use adequate measurements.

skillCards.title: Read logarithmic pH separately from enzyme performance
body: At 25°C, pH 7 is neutral; lower pH is more acidic. Each one-unit decrease represents ten times the hydrogen-ion concentration. Do not read the scale as linear.
